title: What is the primary carbon source for autotrophic (lithotrophic) bacteria?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: What is the primary carbon source for autotrophic (lithotrophic) bacteria?
body.explanation: Autotrophs fix CO₂ as their carbon source. Heterotrophs rely on organic compounds; CO and O₂ are not used as primary carbon sources for cellular biosynthesis.

title: A culture grows only at high salt and needs added vitamins on a simple medium. These two properties identify it respectively as:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A culture grows only at high salt and needs added vitamins on a simple medium. These two properties identify it respectively as:
options: Halophilic and auxotrophic in its needs
body.explanation: Growth at high salt defines a halophile, and an obligate need for externally supplied growth factors (vitamins) defines an auxotroph. The other pairings mismatch the salt and growth-factor requirements described.

title: During the initiation phase of the inflammatory reaction, one characteristic event is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: During the initiation phase of the inflammatory reaction, one characteristic event is:
options: Antibody class switching in B cells
Formation of the membrane attack complex
body.explanation: Early inflammation features vasodilation (and increased permeability), enabling later cell recruitment. Lymphocyte transmigration and class switching are downstream/adaptive events, and MAC formation is a complement effector step, not the defining initiation event.

title: The hepcidin molecule:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The hepcidin molecule:
options: Is synthesized mainly by the kidney
Made by hepatocytes, rising in inflammation
Raises the serum iron when it acts
body.explanation: Hepcidin is a hepatocyte-derived hyposideremic hormone whose level rises in inflammation, degrading ferroportin to lower serum iron. It lowers (not raises) iron and is not made by the kidney.

title: The TCR recognizes antigen only when it is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The TCR recognizes antigen only when it is:
options: In its native, soluble serum form
A free glycolipid circulating in blood
Presented as a peptide bound to MHC
body.explanation: T-cell receptors are MHC-restricted and see processed peptides on MHC. Native soluble antigen is recognized by the BCR, glycolipids are presented by CD1 (to NKT cells), and complement cross-linking is unrelated to TCR recognition.

title: An organism uses nitrate as its terminal electron acceptor in the absence of oxygen. This process is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: An organism uses nitrate as its terminal electron acceptor in the absence of oxygen. This process is:
options: Fermentation with an organic final acceptor
Anaerobic respiration on an inorganic acceptor
body.explanation: Using an inorganic acceptor other than O₂ (here NO₃⁻) to complete an electron transport chain is anaerobic respiration. Aerobic respiration requires O₂, fermentation uses organic acceptors with no ETC, and photophosphorylation is light-driven.

title: Which statement best distinguishes endotoxins from exotoxins?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which statement best distinguishes endotoxins from exotoxins?
options: Exotoxins can never be converted to toxoids
Endotoxins are secreted, highly specific proteins
Endotoxin is wall LPS released on lysis
body.explanation: Endotoxin is the LPS (lipid A) component of the Gram-negative outer membrane, released mainly when cells lyse, with low specificity. Exotoxins are secreted, highly specific, heat-labile proteins that CAN be made into toxoids.

title: A bacterium oxidizes inorganic compounds for energy while using CO₂ as its carbon source. It is best classified as a:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A bacterium oxidizes inorganic compounds for energy while using CO₂ as its carbon source. It is best classified as a:
body.explanation: Chemolithotrophs derive energy from oxidation of inorganic compounds and fix CO₂. Heterotrophs use organic carbon, photoautotrophs use light energy, and auxotrophs are defined by a requirement for specific growth factors they cannot synthesize.

title: Which set of clotting factors is vitamin K–dependent?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which set of clotting factors is vitamin K–dependent?
options: Factors II, VII, IX, and X
Factors V, VIII, XI, and XII
Factors I, V, VIII, and XIII
body.explanation: Vitamin K is needed for γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X (and proteins C and S). Factors I, V, VIII, XI, XII, and XIII are not vitamin K–dependent.

title: Which describes the correct peptide-size preference of MHC molecules?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which describes the correct peptide-size preference of MHC molecules?
options: MHC I binds 8–10 aa, MHC II over 13 aa
MHC I binds over 13 aa, MHC II 8–10 aa
Neither binds peptides, only whole proteins
Both bind peptides of exactly eight aa
body.explanation: The closed groove of MHC I accommodates short 8–10-residue peptides, whereas the open-ended MHC II groove binds longer peptides (>13 aa). The reversed and other options misstate these constraints.

title: The TCR is closely associated with which signaling complex required to transduce activation signals?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The TCR is closely associated with which signaling complex required to transduce activation signals?
body.explanation: CD3 is non-covalently linked to the TCR and transmits the intracellular activation signal. B7 is a co-stimulatory ligand on APCs, Fc receptors bind antibody, and complement receptors bind complement fragments.

title: Which relationship best reflects vitamin B12 function in metabolism?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which relationship best reflects vitamin B12 function in metabolism?
options: Methylmalonic acid forms only with adequate B12
B12 deficiency raises methylmalonic acid, step blocked
B12 deficiency lowers methylmalonic acid markedly
B12 plays no metabolic role at all in this pathway
body.explanation: B12 is a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; deficiency blocks the step and methylmalonic acid accumulates. Thus deficiency raises, not lowers, MMA, and B12 is clearly involved in the pathway.

subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The intrinsic coagulation pathway:
options: Is explored by the prothrombin time
Starts with activation of contact factors
body.explanation: The intrinsic pathway begins with contact-factor activation and is explored by the aPTT. The PT explores the extrinsic pathway, and tissue factor (extrinsic) is the physiological in-vivo trigger, so the other options are incorrect.

body.stem: Erythropoietin is mainly synthesized by the:
body.explanation: The kidney is the principal site of erythropoietin production, increasing output in hypoxic conditions such as high altitude. The liver contributes only minimally (mainly in fetal life).

title: Pattern Recognition Receptors such as TLRs recognize:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Pattern Recognition Receptors such as TLRs recognize:
options: Self peptides displayed on the MHC
Unique epitopes of a single pathogen
body.explanation: PRRs detect conserved PAMPs common to broad microbial classes. They are not clonally distributed and do not recognize unique single-pathogen epitopes or MHC-presented self peptides the way adaptive receptors do.

title: During which bacterial growth phase does the rate of cell division equal the rate of cell death, producing a plateau?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: During which bacterial growth phase does the rate of cell division equal the rate of cell death, producing a plateau?
options: Lag phase, when cells adapt first
body.explanation: In the stationary phase, nutrient depletion balances division against death, so viable counts plateau. The lag phase is adaptation, the exponential phase is net growth, and the death phase is net decline.

title: A specimen cannot be cultured soon after collection. Which medium prevents drying and inhibits overgrowth of undesirable bacteria during transit?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A specimen cannot be cultured soon after collection. Which medium prevents drying and inhibits overgrowth of undesirable bacteria during transit?
body.explanation: Transport media maintain organism viability while preventing desiccation and overgrowth until plating. Enriched media support fastidious growth, differential media distinguish species biochemically, and enrichment broths actively promote a target organism's growth.

title: The chief immunological consequence of the MHC's high, codominantly expressed polymorphism is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The chief immunological consequence of the MHC's high, codominantly expressed polymorphism is:
options: Inability to present any self peptides
A broad peptide repertoire, but graft rejection
Complete loss of MHC restriction of T cells
body.explanation: High, codominant MHC polymorphism lets a population present an enormous range of peptides, but it also creates major allogeneic differences that drive graft rejection. It does not make presentation uniform, abolish self-peptide display, or remove MHC restriction.

title: Without vitamin K a bacterium/host makes inactive coagulation proteins, and vitamin K antagonists anticoagulate. The principle illustrated is that vitamin K:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Without vitamin K a bacterium/host makes inactive coagulation proteins, and vitamin K antagonists anticoagulate. The principle illustrated is that vitamin K:
options: Serves as the terminal electron acceptor
Is a structural unit of peptidoglycan wall
body.explanation: Vitamin K enables γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues, giving these proteins their calcium/phospholipid-binding capacity; without it, inactive precursors result, which is why VKAs anticoagulate. It does not cleave fibrinogen, serve as an electron acceptor, or build peptidoglycan.

title: Integrons contribute to antibiotic resistance primarily because they:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Integrons contribute to antibiotic resistance primarily because they:
options: Are circular elements that are highly stable
Capture, express and spread gene cassettes
body.explanation: Integrons use a site-specific integrase to capture and express mobile gene cassettes, spreading resistance determinants. They do not replicate autonomously, and stability or porin synthesis is not their defining role.

title: A defensin is called a 'natural antibiotic.' The most precise reason, distinguishing it from complement, is that defensins:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A defensin is called a 'natural antibiotic.' The most precise reason, distinguishing it from complement, is that defensins:
options: Require specific antibody in order to be active
Are produced only by liver hepatocytes alone
Are cleavage fragments of complement protein C3
body.explanation: Defensins are cationic antimicrobial peptides that act directly on microbial membranes, independent of the complement cascade or antibody. They are not complement fragments, do not depend on antibody, and are produced by several cell types (e.g., Paneth cells, neutrophils, epithelia).

title: Which compartment of the body holds the largest amount of iron?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which compartment of the body holds the largest amount of iron?
body.explanation: Most body iron is incorporated into hemoglobin within red cells. Storage (ferritin) and myoglobin hold smaller fractions, and the transport pool (transferrin-bound) is the smallest.

body.explanation: Depleted iron stores lower ferritin, making it the key marker of iron deficiency. Ferritin rises in hemochromatosis and inflammation, so 'increased' or 'normal' would not fit true iron deficiency.

subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which component is found in the Gram-negative cell wall but NOT in the Gram-positive cell wall?
options: Teichoic acid threaded through the wall
body.explanation: Lipopolysaccharide (in the outer membrane) is unique to Gram-negative bacteria. A thick peptidoglycan layer, teichoic acid, and lipoteichoic acid are all hallmarks of the Gram-positive wall.

body.stem: Th1 cells mainly produce:
options: IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13, which drive IgE production
body.explanation: Th1: IFN-γ (intracellular microbes); Th2: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 (helminths, allergy); Th17: IL-17 (extracellular bacteria, fungi).

title: An epitope is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: An epitope is:
options: The part of an antigen recognised by an antibody or T-cell receptor
The whole antigen molecule, including its carrier protein and constant parts
The constant region of an antibody
body.explanation: Also called the antigenic determinant; a hapten needs a carrier to be immunogenic.

title: Which bacterial structure is responsible for the transfer of DNA to other cells?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which bacterial structure is responsible for the transfer of DNA to other cells?
options: Pilus, also called the sex pilus
Flagellum, which is used for motility
body.explanation: The (sex) pilus mediates conjugative DNA transfer between bacteria. The flagellum is for motility, fimbriae are short adhesion appendages, and the glycocalyx is an external coat for adhesion/protection.

title: Activation of the platelet prostaglandin pathway is important because it leads to production of:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Activation of the platelet prostaglandin pathway is important because it leads to production of:
body.explanation: In platelets, the pathway yields thromboxane A2, a potent promoter of aggregation and vasoconstriction. Prostacyclin is an endothelial counter-regulator, while plasmin and antithrombin oppose clotting rather than support platelet activation.

title: Hemoglobin synthesis is correctly described as:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Hemoglobin synthesis is correctly described as:
options: Beginning only in the mature red cell
Starting and finishing at the BFU-E stage
Governed by globin genes, balanced α/non-α
Regulated mainly by the oxidative pathway
body.explanation: Globin gene expression governs hemoglobin synthesis, yielding balanced α and non-α (e.g., β) chains plus heme. Synthesis occurs in nucleated erythroid precursors (not the mature, anucleate erythrocyte) and is not controlled by the oxidative pathway.

title: MHC class I molecules present endogenous peptides to which lymphocytes?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: MHC class I molecules present endogenous peptides to which lymphocytes?
body.explanation: MHC I presents endogenous (e.g., viral) peptides to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells. CD4⁺ helper cells recognize MHC II, while B cells and NK cells do not use MHC I peptide presentation in this way.

title: Opsonization functionally enhances immunity by:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Opsonization functionally enhances immunity by:
body.explanation: Opsonins (e.g., C3b, IgG) coat pathogens so phagocytes engulf them more efficiently. Direct lysis is a MAC/complement function, class switching is a B-cell process, and fever is a systemic acute-phase effect.

title: In conjugation, which feature most directly explains why resistance can spread rapidly between unrelated bacteria?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: In conjugation, which feature most directly explains why resistance can spread rapidly between unrelated bacteria?
options: Conjugative plasmids transferred via the sex pilus
Transposons replicating freely in the cytoplasm
Mutations that are induced within the recipient cell
body.explanation: Conjugative plasmids transfer resistance horizontally through the sex pilus, even across species, far faster than mutation plus vertical descent. Mutations are not recipient-induced, transposons are not autonomously replicating, and phage integration describes transduction/lysogeny, not conjugation.

title: A 65-year-old has isolated splenomegaly, Hb 9.5, MCV 90, WBC 40,000 with 88% mature lymphocytes, normal platelets. The likely diagnosis is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A 65-year-old has isolated splenomegaly, Hb 9.5, MCV 90, WBC 40,000 with 88% mature lymphocytes, normal platelets. The likely diagnosis is:
body.explanation: Marked, persistent lymphocytosis of small mature lymphocytes in an older adult with splenomegaly is typical of chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Acute leukemia shows blasts, EBV is usually acute in younger patients with atypical lymphocytes, and myelofibrosis shows a leukoerythroblastic picture rather than pure lymphocytosis.

title: What substance is most commonly used to solidify bacterial culture media?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: What substance is most commonly used to solidify bacterial culture media?
options: Blood, used as an enrichment supplement
Peptone, a nutrient source for broth
body.explanation: Agar is the standard solidifying agent because most bacteria cannot degrade it and it stays solid at incubation temperatures. Gelatin is liquefied by many bacteria, peptone is a nutrient source, and blood is an enrichment supplement rather than a solidifier.

body.stem: A toxoid used in vaccination is best described as:
options: A highly toxic, fully active molecule
A purified fragment of the capsule
A live attenuated strain of bacterium
A toxin inactivated but still immunogenic
body.explanation: A toxoid is a toxin (e.g., treated with formalin) that has lost toxicity but retains antigenicity to elicit protective antibodies. It is not toxic, not a capsule, and not a live organism like BCG.

title: Why does anemia of chronic inflammation resemble iron deficiency on indices yet show HIGH ferritin?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Why does anemia of chronic inflammation resemble iron deficiency on indices yet show HIGH ferritin?
options: Transferrin saturation actually rises quite markedly
Hepcidin rises, trapping iron from erythropoiesis
Erythropoietin output is greatly increased here
Inflammation depletes the total body iron stores
body.explanation: Inflammatory cytokines raise hepcidin, sequestering iron in macrophages/stores (so ferritin is high) while functionally starving erythropoiesis, producing a hypoproliferative, often microcytic picture. Total stores are not depleted, transferrin saturation is typically low, and EPO response is blunted.

title: In the cell-based concept of coagulation, exposure of tissue factor is significant because it:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: In the cell-based concept of coagulation, exposure of tissue factor is significant because it:
options: Is the cofactor support for factor VIII
Directly activates the enzyme plasmin now
body.explanation: Tissue factor exposure activates factor VII and launches the extrinsic pathway, marking the initiation phase of coagulation. It is not the cofactor support for VIII, it is expressed by subendothelial/perivascular cells (not only hepatocytes), and it does not directly activate plasmin.

title: In the cell-based concept of coagulation, the amplification phase is best characterized by:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: In the cell-based concept of coagulation, the amplification phase is best characterized by:
options: Tissue factor exposure starting factor VII
Cross-linking of fibrin by factor XIII
body.explanation: Initial trace thrombin amplifies the response by activating factors V and VIII and further activating platelets, setting up the propagation burst. Tissue factor/VII is the initiation phase, factor XIII cross-linking is stabilization, and plasmin acts in fibrinolysis.

The first step is to review the complete blood count and blood smear

title: Hemostasis is best described as:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Hemostasis is best described as:
options: The normal reaction that stops bleeding
body.explanation: Hemostasis is the physiological response that arrests bleeding at an injury site. It is a multi-step (not single/simple) process, and it produces a localized (not generalized) plug rather than fibrinolysis alone.

title: What is the primary target of aminoglycosides in bacteria?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: What is the primary target of aminoglycosides in bacteria?
body.explanation: Aminoglycosides bind the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA. The 50S subunit is targeted by macrolides/chloramphenicol, the wall by β-lactams/glycopeptides, and the membrane by polymyxins.

title: Which interpretation fits Hb 7.5, MCV 88, WBC 3000 (N 50%, L 40%, M 10%), platelets 120,000?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which interpretation fits Hb 7.5, MCV 88, WBC 3000 (N 50%, L 40%, M 10%), platelets 120,000?
body.explanation: Low Hb with WBC of 3000 indicates anemia plus leukopenia; the differential percentages are roughly normal and platelets are only mildly reduced. The other options misread the white-cell count or red-cell indices.

title: The innate immune response is best characterized as:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The innate immune response is best characterized as:
options: Mediated by a clonal antibody set
body.explanation: Innate immunity acts within hours, is non-specific, and its recognition does not change with exposure. Slow, specific, improving responses with an antibody repertoire describe adaptive immunity.

title: A child with a defect preventing β2-microglobulin association would most directly impair:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A child with a defect preventing β2-microglobulin association would most directly impair:
options: Surface MHC class I and CD8⁺ surveillance
Antibody secretion by the plasma cells
body.explanation: β2-microglobulin is the invariant light chain of MHC class I; without it, MHC I cannot reach the surface, crippling endogenous antigen presentation to CD8⁺ T cells. Antibody secretion, mast-cell function, and complement cleavage do not depend on β2-microglobulin.

subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The three main clinical signs suggesting increased hemolysis are:
body.explanation: Increased red-cell destruction classically produces anemia, jaundice (from bilirubin), and splenomegaly. Fever/purpura, the cardiovascular signs, and the other groupings are not the defining triad of hemolysis.

title: NKT cells are unusual because their semi-invariant TCR recognizes:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: NKT cells are unusual because their semi-invariant TCR recognizes:
options: Free LPS circulating in the plasma
Peptides presented by classical MHC II
Native antigen captured by the BCR
Lipids and glycolipids presented by CD1d
body.explanation: NKT cells recognize (glyco)lipids presented by the non-classical CD1d molecule. Classical MHC presents peptides, LPS is sensed by TLR4, and native-antigen/BCR recognition is a B-cell property.

title: Which molecule is a positively charged antimicrobial peptide that kills microbes by altering membrane permeability?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which molecule is a positively charged antimicrobial peptide that kills microbes by altering membrane permeability?
options: Interferon, which acts on host cells
body.explanation: Defensins are cationic AMPs that aggregate on microbial membranes and form pores. Lysozyme cleaves peptidoglycan, interferons act antivirally on host cells, and lactoferrin sequesters iron rather than forming membrane pores.

title: The complement system contributes to inflammation chiefly through which type of fragment?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The complement system contributes to inflammation chiefly through which type of fragment?
options: Opsonins such as the C3b fragment
Mannose-binding lectin of the lectin pathway
Anaphylatoxins such as C3a and C5a
body.explanation: Anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a) recruit and activate leukocytes and trigger mast-cell degranulation, driving inflammation. C3b is mainly an opsonin, the MAC lyses targets, and mannose-binding lectin initiates the lectin pathway rather than directly mediating inflammation.

title: How does an antibiotic select for resistant bacteria in a population?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: How does an antibiotic select for resistant bacteria in a population?
options: It directly induces brand-new resistance mutations
It transfers resistance genes between cells
It raises the mutation rate of the population
It kills susceptible cells, sparing resistant mutants
body.explanation: Antibiotics do not create resistance; they exert selective pressure that eliminates susceptible cells, leaving pre-existing resistant mutants to multiply. Mutations arise spontaneously, independent of the drug, which does not itself transfer genes.

body.explanation: IgG is carried across by the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn).

subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: TFPI and the antithrombin/protein C–protein S systems share the general role of:
options: Limiting and localizing clotting to injury
body.explanation: Natural anticoagulant inhibitors confine clotting to the injury site and prevent runaway thrombosis. They do not promote fibrin, activate platelets, or degrade vitamin K.

Do not bind MHC at all
body.explanation: Positive selection (cortex) = MHC restriction; negative selection (medulla) removes strongly self-reactive cells.

title: Which feature is a unique structural component of the Gram-negative cell wall, absent in Gram-positives?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which feature is a unique structural component of the Gram-negative cell wall, absent in Gram-positives?
options: Lipoteichoic acid anchored to the membrane
A thick peptidoglycan layer with many cross-links
Teichoic acid threaded throughout the wall
The periplasmic space with an outer membrane
body.explanation: Gram-negative bacteria possess an outer membrane enclosing a periplasmic space, a feature Gram-positives lack. The thick peptidoglycan layer, teichoic acid, and lipoteichoic acid are all characteristic of the Gram-positive wall instead.

subject: subj:immuno1

​ Mixing studies are mandatory for the diagnostic workup

subject: subj:immuno1

It is a positive regulator of thrombopoiesis
Is the specific growth factor of thrombopoiesis

title: Reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis is commonly associated with:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis is commonly associated with:
body.explanation: Reactive thrombocytosis follows infections, inflammation, iron deficiency, or splenectomy. Marrow failure and aplastic anemia lower platelets, and a JAK2 clone defines a primary (clonal) rather than reactive thrombocytosis.

title: Regarding the HLA/MHC system in humans:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Regarding the HLA/MHC system in humans:

it plays a key role in antigen presentation
the MHC II genes code for certain complement molecules
It plays an important role in the killing activity of NK cells

title: Anemia in an adult man is defined by a hemoglobin below:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Anemia in an adult man is defined by a hemoglobin below:
body.explanation: Anemia in adult men is defined as hemoglobin under 13 g/dL (and under 12 g/dL in women). The other thresholds are too low and would miss many genuinely anemic patients.

title: Macrophages bridge innate and adaptive immunity. Which is NOT a typical macrophage function?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Macrophages bridge innate and adaptive immunity. Which is NOT a typical macrophage function?
options: Antigen presentation on MHC class II
Clonal expansion via a rearranged receptor
body.explanation: Macrophages lack a rearranged antigen receptor and do not undergo antigen-specific clonal expansion — that is a lymphocyte property. They do phagocytose (aided by opsonins), secrete cytokines, and present antigen on MHC II.

title: Absorption of vitamin B12 depends on the presence of:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Absorption of vitamin B12 depends on the presence of:
body.explanation: Intrinsic factor, secreted by gastric parietal cells, is required for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Insulin, folate (B9), and erythropoietin are not required for this absorptive step.

title: The respiratory (oxidative) burst of phagocytes depends on:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The respiratory (oxidative) burst of phagocytes depends on:
body.explanation: Its absence causes chronic granulomatous disease.

title: The membrane attack complex is formed by:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The membrane attack complex is formed by:
body.explanation: C5b, C6, C7, C8 and multiple C9 form a pore.

title: Hemostasis:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Hemostasis:
options: Induces a delayed and localized hemostatic plug at the site of the vascular injury
Allows the body to start repairing injuries
Is a single and complex process
Hemostasis is the body’s normal reaction to an injury that causes bleeding

title: Dendritic cells begin maturation upon:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Dendritic cells begin maturation upon:
options: Loss of their MHC II expression
Direct contact with red blood cells
body.explanation: Encounter with pathogens and inflammatory cytokines drives DC maturation, increasing MHC and co-stimulatory expression as they migrate to lymph nodes. Maturation raises (not loses) MHC II, and RBC contact is irrelevant.

title: Which antibiotic class acts directly on the bacterial plasma membrane?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which antibiotic class acts directly on the bacterial plasma membrane?
body.explanation: Polymyxins disrupt the membrane by interacting with LPS/phospholipids, increasing permeability. Aminoglycosides and macrolides target the ribosome, and quinolones inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase.

​ Ferric iron needs to be reduced before its absorption
​ The absorption process is located in the colon
​ Only 10% of dietary iron is absorbed

title: The complement fragment that opsonizes pathogens for phagocytosis is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The complement fragment that opsonizes pathogens for phagocytosis is:
options: C9 of the membrane attack complex
body.explanation: C3b coats pathogens and is recognized by complement receptors on phagocytes, promoting opsonization. C5a and C3a are anaphylatoxins, C1q initiates the classical pathway, and C9 forms the membrane attack complex.

title: The molecules C3a and C5a:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The molecules C3a and C5a:
options: are able to create a chemotactic gradient during the inflammatory response
are anti-microbial peptides altering pathogens’ membranes
are small soluble molecules produced during the complement activation

title: The Hepcidin molecule:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The Hepcidin molecule:

​ Its level is increased in case of inflammation

title: A metastatic-cancer patient develops a hypercoagulable state and then bleeding. The unifying explanation is that malignancy:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A metastatic-cancer patient develops a hypercoagulable state and then bleeding. The unifying explanation is that malignancy:
options: It drives the clotting through a protein C excess state
It only ever causes bleeding and never any clotting at all
It explains both phenomena via a vitamin K excess
A major acquired cause of clotting that consumes factors (DIC)
body.explanation: Cancer is a leading acquired cause of hypercoagulability; widespread activation can consume clotting factors and platelets (as in DIC), converting a thrombotic state into a bleeding one. Cancer is not exclusively a bleeding cause, and neither protein C excess nor vitamin K excess accounts for this dual picture.

title: Endotoxins released by Gram-negative bacteria are recognized by host cells mainly through which receptor complex?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Endotoxins released by Gram-negative bacteria are recognized by host cells mainly through which receptor complex?
options: The CD14, TLR4 and MD2 receptor complex
body.explanation: Lipid A of LPS is sensed by the CD14/TLR4/MD2 complex, triggering inflammatory signaling. Fc receptors bind antibody, mannose receptors bind carbohydrate patterns, and C3b receptors mediate complement-based opsonization.

title: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) by NK cells depends on which receptor binding the Fc of IgG?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) by NK cells depends on which receptor binding the Fc of IgG?
body.explanation: CD16 (FcγRIII) on NK cells binds antibody-coated targets to trigger ADCC. KIRs are inhibitory MHC-I receptors, NK cells lack a TCR, and CD1d presents lipids to NKT cells rather than mediating ADCC.

title: Splenomegaly from portal hypertension most likely causes which CBC change via hypersplenism?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Splenomegaly from portal hypertension most likely causes which CBC change via hypersplenism?
body.explanation: Congestive splenomegaly traps blood cells, classically causing mild thrombocytopenia (and modest cytopenias). It does not characteristically cause lymphocytosis, microcytosis, or a regenerative anemia.

title: A 33-year-old woman with no bleeding history has sudden diffuse cutaneous purpura and epistaxis. This most suggests:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A 33-year-old woman with no bleeding history has sudden diffuse cutaneous purpura and epistaxis. This most suggests:
options: An inherited disorder of primary hemostasis
An acquired disorder of primary hemostasis
body.explanation: Sudden mucocutaneous bleeding (purpura, epistaxis) with no prior history points to an acquired primary-hemostasis problem, e.g., immune thrombocytopenia. The absence of lifelong/familial bleeding argues against inherited disorders, and protein C deficiency causes thrombosis, not bleeding.

title: Co-stimulation through CD40–CD40L (besides B7–CD28) is important because it:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Co-stimulation through CD40–CD40L (besides B7–CD28) is important because it:
options: Converts MHC class I into class II
Replaces the need for antigen recognition
Directly forms the membrane attack complex
body.explanation: CD40–CD40L interactions reinforce the activating dialogue between APCs and T cells, 'licensing' APCs and supporting downstream help. They do not bypass antigen recognition, form the MAC, or interconvert MHC classes.

title: NK cells are classified within innate immunity primarily because they:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: NK cells are classified within innate immunity primarily because they:
options: Lack a TCR or BCR and need no priming
Present antigen on MHC class II
body.explanation: NK cells have neither TCR nor BCR and kill without prior antigen sensitization, hallmark innate traits. They do not present antigen on MHC II or secrete antibodies, and lacking a TCR distinguishes them from T cells.

title: Which enzyme detoxifies the superoxide ion in bacterial cells?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which enzyme detoxifies the superoxide ion in bacterial cells?
body.explanation: Superoxide dismutase converts O₂⁻ to H₂O₂ and O₂. Catalase then handles the resulting H₂O₂; peroxidase reduces peroxides using a substrate, and 'hydroxylase' is not part of this detoxification pathway.

subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Bacterial endospores represent which type of stage in response to adverse conditions?
body.explanation: Endospores are dormant, highly resistant survival structures formed under stress; they are metabolically inactive, not reproductive. They do not enhance metabolism or nutrient uptake.

title: For that patient, the most appropriate first-line investigation is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: For that patient, the most appropriate first-line investigation is:
options: A complete blood count with smear
body.explanation: A CBC (especially the platelet count and smear) is the essential first step in suspected primary-hemostasis bleeding. Specialized vWF assays, factor assays, or flow cytometry are second-line, guided by the initial results.

title: Natural killer (NK) cells kill cells that:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Natural killer (NK) cells kill cells that:
options: Carry antibody on their surface only
Have lost or reduced MHC class I ('missing self')
Express high levels of MHC class I and no stress ligands
body.explanation: Loss of MHC I removes the inhibitory signal; NK cells also kill antibody-coated cells by ADCC.

title: What is the uptake of foreign genetic material directly from the environment by a bacterium called?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: What is the uptake of foreign genetic material directly from the environment by a bacterium called?
options: Transduction, using a phage as vector
body.explanation: Transformation is uptake of naked environmental DNA by a competent cell. Conjugation requires cell-to-cell contact via a pilus, transduction uses a bacteriophage vector, and transposition is movement of mobile elements within a genome.

body.stem: The iron transport protein in the blood is:
body.explanation: Transferrin (siderophyllin) carries iron in plasma. Ferroportin exports iron from cells, ferritin stores iron intracellularly, and hepcidin is a regulatory hormone, not a transporter.

title: In oxygen-dependent killing by phagocytes, the superoxide ion is highly toxic chiefly because it:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: In oxygen-dependent killing by phagocytes, the superoxide ion is highly toxic chiefly because it:
options: Contains no unpaired electrons at all
Is rapidly neutralized by catalase action
Is a stable, chemically inert molecule
body.explanation: Superoxide is a reactive radical that can give rise to even more damaging hydroxyl radicals. It is not stable or inert, it is handled by superoxide dismutase (not directly by catalase), and it possesses an unpaired electron, which underlies its reactivity.

options: Cocci, which are spherical in form
Spirilla, which form rigid helical coils
body.explanation: Cocci are spherical bacteria. Bacilli are rod-shaped, spirilla are rigid corkscrew/helical forms, and vibrios are comma-shaped — none of which are spherical.

​ Is considered as a bleeding disorder

title: A 25-year-old has Hb 10, MCV 65, normal WBC and platelets, low ferritin. Before labeling simple iron deficiency, the microcytosis must prompt exclusion of:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A 25-year-old has Hb 10, MCV 65, normal WBC and platelets, low ferritin. Before labeling simple iron deficiency, the microcytosis must prompt exclusion of:
body.explanation: Marked microcytosis can reflect thalassemia as well as iron deficiency, and the two are distinguished by iron studies (ferritin) — so thalassemia must be considered. Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis, acute hemolysis is usually normo-/macrocytic, and aplastic anemia produces pancytopenia rather than isolated microcytosis.

they recognize glycolipids presented by CD1 molecules

title: The first leukocytes to arrive at a site of acute inflammation are usually:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The first leukocytes to arrive at a site of acute inflammation are usually:
body.explanation: Neutrophils dominate in the first 6-24 hours, then monocytes and macrophages.

title: Leuko-reduction of a red cell component is performed mainly to:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Leuko-reduction of a red cell component is performed mainly to:
options: Adds extra clotting factors into the stored unit
Removes white cells, cutting fever and CMV risk
Concentrates the few platelets that are present
Increases the overall shelf-life of the stored unit
body.explanation: Leuko-reduction removes the majority of leukocytes, lowering febrile non-hemolytic reactions, HLA alloimmunization, and CMV transmission risk. It does not extend shelf life, add factors, or concentrate platelets.

title: Lysozyme contributes to innate defense by:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Lysozyme contributes to innate defense by:
options: Producing type I interferons in cells
body.explanation: Lysozyme hydrolyzes peptidoglycan, damaging bacterial walls. Iron chelation is lactoferrin's role, pore formation is characteristic of defensins, and interferon production is a cytokine response, not a lysozyme function.

​ It is always formed by a chain ɑ and a chain 𝛃

title: The polarization of CD4 T cells in Th17 sub-population:
subject: subj:immuno1

options: is characterized by the production of TNFα by these cells
depends on the nature of the cytokine environment
is characterized by the expression of the transcription factor Tbet
allows the recruitment of polynuclear neutrophils

title: The first antibody produced in a primary immune response is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The first antibody produced in a primary immune response is:
body.explanation: IgM (pentamer) dominates the primary response; IgG dominates the secondary response.

title: MHC class I molecules are expressed on:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: MHC class I molecules are expressed on:
options: All nucleated cells of the body
body.explanation: MHC I is found on essentially all nucleated cells, enabling immune surveillance. MHC II is restricted to APCs, and mature red blood cells (which are anucleate) do not express MHC I.

title: Cross-presentation by dendritic cells is important because it allows:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Cross-presentation by dendritic cells is important because it allows:
options: MHC II to present only endogenous cell peptides
Exogenous antigen onto MHC I, priming CD8⁺ T cells
Complement to activate without any antibody
B cells to bypass antigen recognition completely
body.explanation: Cross-presentation routes exogenous antigen onto MHC I, enabling CD8⁺ cytotoxic priming against pathogens/tumors the DC did not itself synthesize. The other statements misdescribe MHC II loading, B-cell recognition, and complement activation.

title: The classical complement pathway is started by:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The classical complement pathway is started by:
options: Spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 on any cell surface
body.explanation: Classical = antibody (IgM, IgG); lectin = MBL; alternative = spontaneous C3 activation on surfaces.

title: In which temperature range do mesophiles, the most common microbes, typically grow?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: In which temperature range do mesophiles, the most common microbes, typically grow?
body.explanation: Mesophiles grow optimally around body/ambient temperature (≈10–40°C), which includes most human pathogens. 0–20°C describes psychrophiles, 40–65°C thermophiles, and 65–110°C hyperthermophiles.

title: One antigen drives a CD8⁺ response, another a CD4⁺/antibody response. The decisive factor is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: One antigen drives a CD8⁺ response, another a CD4⁺/antibody response. The decisive factor is:
options: The physical size of the whole intact pathogen
The ABO blood group typing of the patient
Whether antigen uses the MHC I or MHC II pathway
The presence of solid agar in the medium
body.explanation: Endogenously synthesized (e.g., viral) antigens load onto MHC I for CD8⁺ responses, whereas phagocytosed exogenous antigens load onto MHC II for CD4⁺ help and antibody production. Pathogen size, blood group, and culture conditions do not govern this routing.

title: During an allergic response, degranulation of the basophile occurs upon:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: During an allergic response, degranulation of the basophile occurs upon:
options: BCR stimulation by repeated molecular motifs of allergens at its surface
IgM polymerization by allergens at its surface
IgE bridging by allergens at its surface
binding of allergens directly to the PRRs at its surface
direct binding of allergens to the BCR at its surface

title: Which classification of antibiotics is based on the chemical structure of the compounds?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which classification of antibiotics is based on the chemical structure of the compounds?
options: Mode of action on the target
body.explanation: Grouping by chemical nature (e.g., β-lactams, aminoglycosides) is a structure-based classification. Spectrum, mode of action, and the static/cidal distinction classify antibiotics by effect rather than structure.

title: Which fragment of an immunoglobulin carries the antigen-binding (antibody) function?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which fragment of an immunoglobulin carries the antigen-binding (antibody) function?
body.explanation: The Fab fragment contains the variable regions that bind antigen. The Fc fragment mediates effector functions, the hinge provides flexibility, and the J chain links polymeric immunoglobulins.

title: MHC class I molecules:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: MHC class I molecules:
options: Present extracellular peptides to CD4+ T cells
Are found only on antigen-presenting cells and present extracellular peptides to CD4+ T cells
Are absent from all human cells
Are found on all nucleated cells and present peptides to CD8+ T cells
body.explanation: Class I presents cytosolic (endogenous) peptides to CD8+; class II (APCs) presents exogenous peptides to CD4+.

title: A patient is infected by an organism that produces toxins WITHOUT first colonizing host tissue. This best describes:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A patient is infected by an organism that produces toxins WITHOUT first colonizing host tissue. This best describes:
body.explanation: When pre-formed toxin causes disease without bacterial colonization, the process is an intoxication/toxi-infection. The other options require the organism to first establish itself in the host, and commensalism is non-pathogenic.

title: A direct Coombs test detects:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A direct Coombs test detects:
options: Free antibodies against red cell antigens in the patient's serum
Antibodies or complement already bound to the patient's red cells
body.explanation: The indirect Coombs test detects free antibodies in serum (e.g. antenatal screening, cross-matching).

title: Regarding defensins:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Regarding defensins:
options: ​ They have a microbicidal effect by altering the permeability of microbial membranes
​ They are produced only by epithelial cells
​ They are fragments of the complement

title: Why does the cytoplasmic membrane's selective permeability matter for resistance to heavy metals and detergents?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Why does the cytoplasmic membrane's selective permeability matter for resistance to heavy metals and detergents?
options: It controls solute entry and effluxes toxins
It produces the flagellar H antigen for typing
It forms the periplasmic space of Gram-positives
body.explanation: The membrane's selective permeability and transport systems control solute entry and can exclude or pump out toxic compounds, contributing to resistance. Peptidoglycan synthesis, H-antigen production (a flagellar property), and the periplasmic space (a Gram-negative feature) are distinct functions.

title: A young woman has Hb 10, MCV 65, MCH 22, MCHC 28%, WBC 4000, platelets 6 G/L. Beyond microcytic anemia, the most urgent abnormality is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A young woman has Hb 10, MCV 65, MCH 22, MCHC 28%, WBC 4000, platelets 6 G/L. Beyond microcytic anemia, the most urgent abnormality is:
options: Reactive lymphocytosis worth a brief note
Marked thrombocytosis of the platelet count
Mild leukopenia, really of little concern
body.explanation: A platelet count of 6 G/L is profound, life-threatening thrombocytopenia and the priority finding. The white count is essentially normal, and the platelet value is the opposite of thrombocytosis.

title: Full activation of a naïve T lymphocyte requires at least:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Full activation of a naïve T lymphocyte requires at least:
options: Direct complement binding to the cell
body.explanation: Signal 1 (peptide–MHC/TCR) plus signal 2 (co-stimulation, e.g., B7–CD28) are both needed; signal 1 alone causes anergy. Cytokines provide signal 3 (polarization) but cannot substitute for co-stimulation, and complement is not a T-cell activation signal.

title: Which finding is characteristic of iron deficiency anemia on the CBC?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which finding is characteristic of iron deficiency anemia on the CBC?
body.explanation: Iron deficiency produces microcytic, hypochromic red cells, so MCH is low. MCV is low (not high), transferrin saturation falls, and ferritin is decreased rather than elevated.

title: The B-cell receptor (BCR) differs fundamentally from PRRs because it:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The B-cell receptor (BCR) differs fundamentally from PRRs because it:
options: Requires the CD1 molecules for its presentation
Recognizes conserved patterns shared by microbes
Is identical on every single circulating B cell
body.explanation: The BCR binds native (unprocessed) antigen and varies clonally from cell to cell, hallmarks of adaptive recognition. PRRs (not the BCR) recognize conserved patterns; CD1 presents lipids to NKT cells; and BCRs are not identical across B cells.

title: Von Willebrand factor binds platelets primarily through which platelet surface glycoprotein?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Von Willebrand factor binds platelets primarily through which platelet surface glycoprotein?
body.explanation: vWF tethers platelets to subendothelium via GPIb, the key adhesion step. GPIIb/IIIa (the fibrinogen receptor) mediates aggregation, and GPVI binds collagen, not vWF.

title: The macrophage is a typical cell of innate immunity which ensures:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The macrophage is a typical cell of innate immunity which ensures:
options: ​ Netosis after activation of NADPH oxidase
​ Cytotoxicity by Fas-Fas Ligand death receptors

title: Which list correctly groups probable causes of microcytic anemia?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which list correctly groups probable causes of microcytic anemia?
options: Aplastic anemia as the sole cause
Vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, myelodysplasia
body.explanation: Microcytic anemias classically include iron deficiency, thalassemia, and anemia of chronic inflammation. B12/folate deficiency and myelodysplasia cause macrocytosis, and acute hemolysis is typically normo- or macrocytic.

title: Why are dendritic cells, rather than macrophages, considered the key initiators of the response to a brand-new pathogen?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Why are dendritic cells, rather than macrophages, considered the key initiators of the response to a brand-new pathogen?
options: They are the only cell type expressing MHC class I
They cannot phagocytose at all and only present
They secrete antibodies once they have fully matured
They capture antigen, mature and prime naïve T cells
body.explanation: DCs uniquely sample peripheral tissue, mature, and traffic to secondary lymphoid organs to prime naïve T cells. MHC I is on all nucleated cells, DCs do phagocytose, and they do not secrete antibodies (a plasma-cell function).

title: Professional antigen-presenting cells include macrophages, B lymphocytes, and:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Professional antigen-presenting cells include macrophages, B lymphocytes, and:
body.explanation: Dendritic cells are the third professional APC and the only one able to prime naïve T cells. Erythrocytes and platelets are not APCs, and neutrophils are phagocytes that do not classically prime naïve T cells.

title: A CBC shows Hb 8.5 g/dL, MCV 75 fL, MCH 22 pg, MCHC 27%. The best interpretation is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A CBC shows Hb 8.5 g/dL, MCV 75 fL, MCH 22 pg, MCHC 27%. The best interpretation is:
body.explanation: Low Hb with low MCV and low MCH/MCHC indicates a microcytic, hypochromic anemia (classically iron deficiency). Macrocytic would show high MCV, and the values clearly indicate anemia rather than polycythemia or a normocytic picture.

title: A dendritic cell presents antigen to a naïve T cell but gives NO co-stimulatory signal. The likely outcome is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A dendritic cell presents antigen to a naïve T cell but gives NO co-stimulatory signal. The likely outcome is:
options: Robust Th1 polarization of the cell
body.explanation: Signal 1 without signal 2 induces anergy, a state of unresponsiveness. Effective polarization, B-cell help, and complement activation all require proper activation that co-stimulation enables.

title: Which antibiotic family is generally bactericidal, targets the cell wall, and is inactivated by penicillinase-producing organisms?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which antibiotic family is generally bactericidal, targets the cell wall, and is inactivated by penicillinase-producing organisms?
body.explanation: β-lactams inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking and are hydrolyzed by penicillinases (β-lactamases). Tetracyclines and macrolides are protein-synthesis inhibitors, and aminoglycosides, though they target the ribosome, are not the penicillinase substrate described.

title: The lactoferrin is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: The lactoferrin is:
options: a member of the PRR family
an enzyme contained in the azurophilic granules of the neutrophil
a physiological barrier of the innate immune response
an antimicrobial peptide that inhibits bacterial growth by converting divalent iron (Fe2+) to monovalent iron (Fe+)

title: Which group of bacteria is unable to use oxygen and cannot survive in its presence?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which group of bacteria is unable to use oxygen and cannot survive in its presence?
body.explanation: Obligate anaerobes neither use oxygen nor tolerate it. Facultative anaerobes use oxygen but survive without it, microaerophiles need low O₂, and aerotolerant anaerobes don't use O₂ but survive in its presence.

title: Which virulence factor masks bacterial surface structures and prevents phagocytosis?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which virulence factor masks bacterial surface structures and prevents phagocytosis?
options: Coagulase, which clots the host plasma
body.explanation: The polysaccharide capsule shields surface antigens and resists engulfment by phagocytes. Adhesins mediate attachment, while coagulase and collagenase are enzymes acting on host substrates rather than anti-phagocytic coats.

title: Which cell is the main antigen-presenting cell for naive T cells?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Which cell is the main antigen-presenting cell for naive T cells?
body.explanation: Dendritic cells are the most effective activators of naive T cells.

title: γδ T lymphocytes differ from conventional αβ T cells in that they:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: γδ T lymphocytes differ from conventional αβ T cells in that they:
options: Express a very broad, diverse TCR set
Are the most abundant circulating T cells
Are completely unable to make cytokines
body.explanation: γδ T cells are rare in blood, concentrated at epithelial surfaces, recognize antigen without classical MHC restriction, and have a limited repertoire — yet they still produce cytokines and exert cytotoxicity. The other statements describe αβ T cells or are simply false.

title: A patient on a vitamin K antagonist has a prolonged PT. The best mechanistic explanation is that the drug:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A patient on a vitamin K antagonist has a prolonged PT. The best mechanistic explanation is that the drug:
options: Lowers factors II, VII, IX, X, with VII falling first
Destroys the circulating platelets in the blood
Directly inhibits the active enzyme thrombin itself
Activates plasma antithrombin to block clotting
body.explanation: VKAs impair γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X; because factor VII (extrinsic pathway) has the shortest half-life, the PT prolongs earliest. VKAs do not directly inhibit thrombin, destroy platelets, or activate antithrombin (that is heparin's mechanism).

title: Secretory IgA is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Secretory IgA is:
options: A pentamer joined by a J chain, found mostly in serum
A dimer with a J chain and secretory component
body.explanation: It protects mucosal surfaces and is present in breast milk.

title: Why does a 3rd-generation cephalosporin retain activity against Enterobacter where a 1st-generation agent fails?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Why does a 3rd-generation cephalosporin retain activity against Enterobacter where a 1st-generation agent fails?
options: It disrupts the cytoplasmic membrane directly
It has a broad spectrum and β-lactamase stability
It binds the 30S ribosomal subunit instead
It inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase
body.explanation: Third-generation cephalosporins have a broadened Gram-negative spectrum and improved stability to many β-lactamases, covering organisms like Enterobacter that earlier generations miss. They remain wall-synthesis inhibitors, not ribosome, gyrase, or membrane agents.

title: Thrombopoietin is:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Thrombopoietin is:
options: Synthesized mainly by the thyroid gland
body.explanation: Thrombopoietin is the principal, specific positive regulator of platelet production and is synthesized largely by the liver. It does not come from the thyroid, does not inhibit thrombopoiesis, and is not produced solely by megakaryocytes.

title: Pattern recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors recognise:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Pattern recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors recognise:
options: Specific peptide-MHC complexes presented by dendritic cells
body.explanation: They belong to innate immunity, e.g. TLR4 recognises LPS.

title: A neutropenic post-chemotherapy patient is infected by an organism from his own gut flora. This is best categorized as:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A neutropenic post-chemotherapy patient is infected by an organism from his own gut flora. This is best categorized as:
options: A true-pathogen infection in a healthy host
body.explanation: Disease caused by the host's own microbiota when defenses are impaired is an endogenous opportunistic infection. It is not acquired from outside (exogenous), not transmitted mother-to-child (vertical), and opportunists are by definition not classic true pathogens in healthy hosts.

title: TLR engagement by viral nucleic acids characteristically triggers production of which antiviral mediators?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: TLR engagement by viral nucleic acids characteristically triggers production of which antiviral mediators?
body.explanation: TLR signaling (notably via the TRIF/IRF3 pathway) induces type I interferons that establish an antiviral state. Lysozyme/lactoferrin are constitutive antimicrobials, histamine/serotonin are mast-cell mediators, and clotting factors are unrelated to this output.

title: A virus-infected cell downregulates surface MHC class I to evade CD8⁺ T cells. Why does this make it MORE susceptible to NK killing?
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: A virus-infected cell downregulates surface MHC class I to evade CD8⁺ T cells. Why does this make it MORE susceptible to NK killing?
options: Loss of MHC I removes the inhibitory KIR signal
NK cells need MHC I to bind their antigen
MHC I loss directly activates the BCR
Loss of MHC I raises co-stimulatory signals
body.explanation: NK killing is restrained by inhibitory KIRs engaging self MHC I; when MHC I is lost ('missing self'), inhibition is released and the activating signal dominates, so the cell is killed. The other options misstate NK biology.

title: During phagocytosis, the oxidative stress within neutrophils:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: During phagocytosis, the oxidative stress within neutrophils:
options: induces microbicidy by proteases and anti-microbial peptides
stimulates antibody synthesis by B lymphocytes
induces expression of Fas/FasL death receptors on the cell surface of NK cells
induces oxidation of microbial membranes and lysis of pathogens

title: Immunological memory is a feature of:
subject: subj:immuno1

body.stem: Immunological memory is a feature of:
body.explanation: Memory B and T cells give faster, stronger secondary responses; this is the basis of vaccination.
